chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
"There is no harm in a man sleeping between two female slaves and two free women; indeed, your women are like playthings."
From him, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Abdillah ibn Ja'far, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Mutahhar who said:

"I wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Askari (peace be upon him) that I had married four women and did not ask about their names, then I intended to divorce one of them and marry another woman. He (peace be upon him) wrote back: 'Look for a distinguishing mark; if it is on one of them, say: 'Bear witness that so-and-so, who has such and such a mark, is divorced.' Then marry the other when the waiting period has ended.'"
ai.seo_question: How to identify a specific wife for divorce when her name is unknown according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the flexibility of Shia jurisprudence in domestic matters, where the first narration uses the metaphor of 'playthings' to denote the permissibility of cohabitation with multiple wives or concubines without restriction. The second narration provides a practical legal mechanism for identifying a specific wife for divorce when names are unknown, emphasizing the use of physical marks ('alamah') to ensure the validity of the talaq before remarriage. These rulings highlight the pragmatic approach of the Imams in managing polygamous households and the procedural nuances of divorce in early Islamic society.
